claim: RIPK1 and RIPK3 play important roles in diverse innate immune pathways.
source: Receptor interacting protein kinases (RIPK) RIPK1 and RIPK3 play important roles in diverse innate immune pathways.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the broader scientific literature and the subsequent findings in the manuscript.

claim: Some RIPK1/3-associated proteins are absent in specific vertebrate lineages.
source: Despite this, some RIPK1/3-associated proteins are absent in specific vertebrate lineages, suggesting that some RIPK1/3 functions are conserved, while others are more evolutionarily labile.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenomic analysis data presented in Figure 1C and discussed throughout the manuscript.

claim: RIPK3 and RIPK1 undergo lineage-specific rapid evolution.
source: Here, we perform comparative evolutionary analyses of RIPK1–5 and associated proteins in vertebrates to identify lineage-specific rapid evolution of RIPK3 and RIPK1 and recurrent loss of RIPK3-associated proteins.
evidence: This is supported by positive selection analysis shown in Figure 1B and discussed in the Results section.

claim: Diverse vertebrate RIPK3 proteins are able to activate NF-κB and cell death in human cells.
source: Despite this, diverse vertebrate RIPK3 proteins are able to activate NF-κB and cell death in human cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: The RIP homotypic interaction motif (RHIM) in RIPK3 is strikingly conserved.
source: Additional analyses revealed a striking conservation of the RIP homotypic interaction motif (RHIM) in RIPK3, as well as other human RHIM-containing proteins.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Diversity in the RIPK3 RHIM can tune activation of NF-κB while retaining the ability to activate cell death.
source: Interestingly, diversity in the RIPK3 RHIM can tune activation of NF-κB while retaining the ability to activate cell death.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and 4F.

claim: NF-κB activation is a core, conserved function of RIPK3.
source: Altogether, these data suggest that NF-κB activation is a core, conserved function of RIPK3, and the RHIM can tailor RIPK3 function to specific needs within and between species.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing NF-κB activation by diverse vertebrate RIPK3 proteins.

claim: RIPK3 and RIPK1 interact via their shared RHIM to form amyloid-like aggregates.
source: Downstream of signals from innate immune receptors like Z-DNA binding protein 1 (ZBP1) and tumor necrosis factor receptor 1 (TNFR1), RIPK3, and RIPK1 interact via their shared RIP homotypic interaction motif (RHIM) to form amyloid-like aggregates (Wu et al., 2021), leading to their autophosphorylation and activation of additional effector proteins to carry out their innate immune functions.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wu et al., 2021.

claim: RIPK3 can phosphorylate MLKL to activate necroptosis.
source: For example, RIPK3 can phosphorylate MLKL to activate highly inflammatory programmed necrotic cell death (necroptosis) (Sun et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sun et al., 2012.

claim: RIPK1/3 can engage caspase-8 to activate apoptotic caspases.
source: RIPK1/3 can engage caspase-8 (CASP8) to activate apoptotic caspases (Wang et al., 2008; Mandal et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2008 and Mandal et al., 2014.

claim: RIPK1/3 can activate the pro-survival and pro-inflammatory transcription factor NF-κB.
source: or RIPK1/3 can activate the pro-survival and pro-inflammatory transcription factor NF-κB (Meylan et al., 2004; Moriwaki et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Meylan et al., 2004 and Moriwaki et al., 2014.

claim: RIPK3 is evolutionarily dynamic in vertebrates.
source: Like many innate immune proteins, RIPK3 is evolutionarily dynamic in vertebrates.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenomic and evolutionary analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: RIPK3 and associated proteins ZBP1 and MLKL have been lost in some vertebrate lineages, including birds, carnivores, and marsupials.
source: Phylogenomic analyses of a small number of species from different vertebrate clades suggest that RIPK3 and the associated proteins ZBP1 and MLKL have been lost in some vertebrate lineages, including birds, carnivores, and marsupials (Dondelinger et al., 2016; Águeda-Pinto et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dondelinger et al., 2016 and Águeda-Pinto et al., 2021, and confirmed by data in Figure 1C.

claim: RIPK3, RIPK1, MLKL, and ZBP1 interact with viral proteins.
source: In addition, RIPK3, RIPK1, MLKL, and ZBP1 are known to interact with viral proteins (Harris et al., 2015; Croft et al., 2018; Wagner et al., 2015; Muscolino et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: RIPK3, RIPK1, MLKL, and ZBP1 are evolving under recurrent positive selection in primates and bats.
source: and have been shown to be evolving under recurrent positive selection in both primates and bats (Palmer et al., 2021; Cariou et al., 2022), a hallmark of host proteins that directly interact with viral proteins (Daugherty and Malik, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Palmer et al., 2021, Cariou et al., 2022, and Daugherty and Malik, 2012.

claim: There are known differences between humans and mice in the roles of specific genes in the regulation of NF-κB.
source: Even between humans and mice, there are known differences in the roles of specific genes in the regulation of NF-κB, suggesting this pathway can be tailored to the distinct environments of different species (Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2017.

claim: RIPK1 and RIPK3 are part of a larger family of RIPKs, including RIPK2, RIPK4, and ANKK1/RIPK5.
source: Furthermore, RIPK1 and RIPK3 are part of a larger family of RIPKs, including RIPK2, RIPK4, and ANKK1/RIPK5, which, with the exception of RIPK5, are known to activate NF-κB in various cellular contexts (Cuny and Degterev, 2021; Eng et al., 2021; Lv et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cuny and Degterev, 2021, Eng et al., 2021, and Lv et al., 2022.

claim: Human RIPK1–4 activate NF-κB through different mechanisms.
source: Human RIPK1–4 activate NF-κB, albeit through different mechanisms, including differential dependence on endogenous RIPK1 and kinase activity (Figure 1—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 1–3.

claim: RIPK5 does not activate NF-κB.
source: Interestingly, despite its close homology to RIPK4, RIPK5 did not activate NF-κB.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Only RIPK1 and RIPK3 show evidence of recurrent positive selection among RIPK1–5.
source: Notably, we only found evidence for positive selection acting on RIPK1 and RIPK3 (Figure 1B, Supplementary files 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by positive selection analysis data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In primates, RIPK3 is evolving under strong positive selection, while RIPK1 is not.
source: For instance, in primates, RIPK3 is evolving under strong positive selection, while RIPK1 is not, consistent with previous data (Palmer et al., 2021; Cariou et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1B and citations to Palmer et al., 2021 and Cariou et al., 2022.

claim: In ungulates, RIPK3 does not show evidence for positive selection, whereas RIPK1 does.
source: In contrast, ungulate RIPK3 does not show evidence for positive selection, whereas ungulate RIPK1 does.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: RIPK3, ZBP1, and MLKL are lost in birds.
source: We first confirmed the loss of necroptosis-associated proteins that has been previously reported (Dondelinger et al., 2016): RIPK3 and ZBP1 in birds
evidence: This is supported by phylogenomic data in Figure 1C and citation to Dondelinger et al., 2016.

claim: RIPK3, ZBP1, and MLKL are lost in marsupials.
source: RIPK3, ZBP1, and MLKL in marsupials
evidence: This is supported by phylogenomic data in Figure 1C.

claim: MLKL is lost in carnivores.
source: MLKL in carnivores.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenomic data in Figure 1C.

claim: ZBP1 is absent in all fish species.
source: In addition, we found that ZBP1 is absent in all fish species, suggesting that this protein, and ZBP1-mediated necroptosis, arose only during tetrapod evolution.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenomic data in Figure 1C.

claim: RIPK1 is found in nearly every vertebrate genome queried.
source: RIPK1 is found nearly every vertebrate genome queried
evidence: This is supported by phylogenomic data in Figure 1C.

claim: Clear RIPK1 homologs were identified in several non-vertebrate species, including zebra mussel, several spiralia species, and lancelet species.
source: and clear RIPK1 homologs were identified in several non-vertebrate species, including zebra mussel (Dreissena polymorpha), several additional spiralia species, and lancelet species in the genus Branchiostoma (accession numbers in Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenomic analysis data.

claim: At least one copy of CASP8/10 is found in most vertebrate genomes.
source: At least one copy of CASP8/10 is found in most vertebrate genomes.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenomic data in Figure 1C.

claim: Two copies of CASP8/10 began in tetrapods, coinciding with the emergence of ZBP1.
source: Two copies, presumably marking the delineation between CASP8 and CASP10, began in tetrapod, coinciding with the emergence of ZBP1.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenomic data in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Suborder Myomorpha and Castorimorpha rodents have lost CASP10, whereas Sciuromorpha and Hystricomorpha rodents have retained CASP10.
source: We also confirmed the loss of CASP10 in some rodents (Eckhart et al., 2008) (see Figure 1—figure supplement 4A for CASP8/10 breakdown), revealing that suborder Myomorpha ('mouse-like') and Castorimorpha ('beaver-like') rodents have lost CASP10, whereas Sciuromorpha ('squirrel-like') and Hystricomorpha ('porcupine-like') rodents have retained CASP10.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenomic data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A and citation to Eckhart et al., 2008.

claim: FADD and TRIF are well conserved in all vertebrates.
source: Finally, we found that FADD and TRIF are well conserved in all vertebrates.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenomic data in Figure 1C.

claim: A second paralog of RIPK2, called RIPK2B, exists in many vertebrates but is lost in therian mammals.
source: Intriguingly, we observed a second paralog of RIPK2, which we call RIPK2B, in many vertebrates but lost in therian (live-bearing) mammals (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenomic data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: NOD2 is present in lamprey and fish, but absent in birds, reptiles, and some amphibians.
source: NOD2 is present in lamprey and fish, but absent in birds, reptiles, and some amphibians, including some of the same species that contain RIPK2B.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenomic data in Figure 1C.

claim: RIPK4 is present in jawed vertebrates.
source: RIPK4 is present in jawed vertebrates.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenomic data in Figure 1C.

claim: IRF6 emerged prior to RIPK4 and has been lost in many vertebrate species, particularly in carnivores, cetaceans, and ungulates.
source: IRF6, the only known phosphorylation target of RIPK4 (Cuny and Degterev, 2021; Eng et al., 2021), emerged prior to RIPK4 and has been lost in many vertebrate species, particularly in carnivores, cetaceans, and ungulates.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenomic data in Figure 1C and citations.

claim: RIPK5 has been lost in several lineages, including monotremes and lagomorphs.
source: RIPK5, which has no known function and no known interacting proteins, has been lost in several lineages, including monotremes and lagomorphs.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenomic data in Figure 1C.

claim: Among all vertebrates tested, only pig and sea lamprey RIPK3 failed to activate NF-κB in human cells.
source: To our surprise, among all vertebrates tested, only pig and sea lamprey RIPK3 failed to activate NF-κB in human cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2B.

claim: Mammalian RIPK3 activation is dependent on RIPK1.
source: Interestingly, while mammalian RIPK3 activation is dependent on RIPK1, both lizard and turtle RIPK3 activate NF-κB independently of RIPK1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2B.

claim: Lizard and turtle RIPK3 activate NF-κB independently of RIPK1.
source: Interestingly, while mammalian RIPK3 activation is dependent on RIPK1, both lizard and turtle RIPK3 activate NF-κB independently of RIPK1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2B.

claim: Most mammalian RIPK3 proteins were able to activate cell death using human ZBP1 and MLKL.
source: Most mammalian RIPK3 proteins were able to activate cell death using human ZBP1 and MLKL (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2C.

claim: Pig RIPK3 is unable to activate NF-κB but can activate cell death.
source: This included pig RIPK3, which is unable to activate NF-κB, suggesting that activation of cell death and NF-κB by RIPK3 proteins has been separated in a species-specific manner.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: Cat RIPK3 can activate NF-κB but fails to activate cell death.
source: Likewise, we observed that cat RIPK3 can activate NF-κB but fails to activate cell death.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: Feline RIPK3 has a mutated kinase catalytic residue.
source: Based on this observation, we analyzed the sequences of carnivore RIPK3 proteins and found that feline RIPK3 has mutated kinase catalytic residue (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), explaining the loss of cell death activation by cat RIPK3.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Only lizard RIPK3 was able to activate cell death among non-mammalian vertebrates tested.
source: Outside of mammals, only lizard RIPK3 was able to activate cell death, despite the ability of both lizard and turtle RIPK3 to activate NF-κB, further suggesting that these functions of RIPK3 have distinct, species-specific requirements.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2C.

claim: There is a cluster of rapidly evolving sites in and around the C-terminal RHIM of primate RIPK3.
source: While we identified rapidly evolving sites throughout the primate RIPK3, there was a cluster of sites in and around the C-terminal RHIM (Figure 3, Supplementary file 5), which is a known region of interaction between RIPK1 and RIPK3 and RIPK3 homooligomerization (Wu et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by positive selection analysis data in Figure 3A and citations.

claim: The core RHIM tetrad (VQVG) in primate RIPK3 is not rapidly evolving.
source: Intriguingly, despite multiple rapidly evolving sites within the RHIM, a core tetrad (VQVG) is not rapidly evolving.
evidence: This is supported by positive selection analysis data in Figure 3A.

claim: The core tetrads of bat and carnivore RIPK3 are not rapidly evolving.
source: Similarly, the core tetrads of bat and carnivore RIPK3 are not rapidly evolving (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by positive selection analysis data in Figure 3B.

claim: The RIPK3 core RHIM tetrad is highly conserved across vertebrates.
source: Furthermore, the RIPK3 core RHIM tetrad is highly conserved across vertebrates (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data in Figure 3C.

claim: Mutation of the RIPK3 RHIM core tetrad reduced activation of NF-κB in human, mouse, and cat RIPK3.
source: Mutation of human, mouse, and cat RIPK3 RHIMs reduced activation of NF-κB as expected (Figure 3D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3D.

claim: Activation of NF-κB by lizard and turtle RIPK3 is dependent on the RHIM despite being independent of RIPK1.
source: Surprisingly, despite activating independently of RIPK1 (Figure 2B), activation of NF-κB by lizard and turtle RIPK3 remains dependent on the RHIM (Figure 3E, left) and independent of RIPK3 kinase activity (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: The sea lamprey RHIM diverges from the canonical V/I-Q-V/I-G tetrad and contains TQIG.
source: Interestingly, while analyzing RHIM domains of nonhuman RIPK3, we observed that the sea lamprey RHIM diverges from the canonical V/I-Q-V/I-G tetrad and instead contains TQIG (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data in Figure 3C.

claim: Mutating the sea lamprey RIPK3 RHIM from TQIG to IQIG increases NF-κB activation.
source: To determine if this was responsible for the limited activation of NF-κB by sea lamprey RIPK3, we mutated this motif to IQIG and observed an increase in NF-κB activation (Figure 3E, right).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3E.

claim: The RIPK1 RHIM is highly conserved in vertebrates and in RIPK1-like proteins found in zebra mussel, Lingula species, and multiple lancelet species.
source: We found that the RIPK1 RHIM is highly conserved in vertebrates and in RIPK1-like proteins found in zebra mussel, Lingula species, and multiple lancelet species (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data in Figure 4A.

claim: Diverse vertebrate RIPK1CT proteins activate NF-κB independent of endogenous RIPK1.
source: Diverse vertebrate RIPK1CT proteins activate NF-κB independent of endogenous RIPK1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), consistent with our hypothesis that NF-κB activation is an ancestral and conserved function of these proteins.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Mutation of the RHIM domain does not affect activation of NF-κB by mammalian RIPK1CT proteins.
source: Specifically, mutation of the RHIM domain does not affect activation of NF-κB by mammalian proteins, including human, mouse, cat, and pig (Figure 4B, left).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4B.

claim: Mutation of the RHIM domain attenuated or completely prevented the ability of non-mammalian RIPK1CT to activate NF-κB.
source: In contrast, mutation of the RHIM domain attenuated or completely prevented the ability of non-mammalian (lizard, sea lamprey, and zebra mussel) RIPK1CT to activate NF-κB (Figure 4B, right).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4B.

claim: The first RHIM of ZBP1 is highly conserved in mammals and some other tetrapods, whereas the second RHIM diverges even within mammals.
source: The TRIF RHIM and the first RHIM of ZBP1 are also highly conserved in mammals and some other tetrapods, whereas the second RHIM of ZBP1 diverges even within mammals (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data in Figure 4C.

claim: ZBP1 activates NF-κB in a RHIM- and RIPK1-dependent manner.
source: As described previously (Rebsamen et al., 2009), ZBP1 activates NF-κB in a RHIM- and RIPK1-dependent manner (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4D and citation to Rebsamen et al., 2009.

claim: Only the first RHIM tetrad of ZBP1 is required for NF-κB activation.
source: Consistent with our evolutionary prediction, only the first RHIM tetrad is required for NF-κB activation by ZBP1 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4D.

claim: Mutation of the TRIF RHIM domain does not affect activation of NF-κB.
source: Conversely, mutation of the TRIF RHIM domain does not affect activation of NF-κB, and activation is only moderately reduced in RIPK1 KO cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B and C), likely due to the TIR domain in TRIF that is known to mediate its innate immune signaling (Nanson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4—figure supplement 4B and C and citation to Nanson et al., 2019.

claim: Most naturally occurring RHIM tetrad variants activate NF-κB compared to the inactive RIPK3 RHIM mutant, albeit lower than the WT tetrad.
source: Interestingly, while most tested variants activate NF-κB compared to the inactive RIPK3 RHIM mutant (AAAA tetrad), albeit lower than the WT (VQVG) tetrad, TQIG and VQSG did not activate NF-κB (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplements 5 and 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplements 5 and 6.

claim: TQIG and VQSG RHIM tetrad variants did not activate NF-κB.
source: Interestingly, while most tested variants activate NF-κB compared to the inactive RIPK3 RHIM mutant (AAAA tetrad), albeit lower than the WT (VQVG) tetrad, TQIG and VQSG did not activate NF-κB (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplements 5 and 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4E.

claim: All RHIM tetrad variants were able to activate ZBP1-dependent cell death similar to WT RIPK3.
source: All tetrad variants were able to activate ZBP1-dependent cell death similar to WT RIPK3 (Figure 4F), further revealing the separation of RIPK3-mediated NF-κB activation from cell death activation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4F.

claim: NF-κB is a deeply conserved pathway in many metazoans.
source: Activation of NF-κB is critical to both the innate and adaptive immune response in humans and mice (Zhang et al., 2017) and is a deeply conserved pathway in many metazoans (Wang et al., 2006; Hetru and Hoffmann, 2009; Williams and Gilmore, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2006, Hetru and Hoffmann, 2009, and Williams and Gilmore, 2020.

claim: Necroptosis is hypothesized to have arisen in vertebrates.
source: It is hypothesized that necroptosis, defined by RIPK3-mediated activation of MLKL, arose in vertebrates (Dondelinger et al., 2016; Tummers and Green, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dondelinger et al., 2016 and Tummers and Green, 2022.

claim: Two critical regulators of necroptosis, CASP8 and ZBP1, are only found in tetrapods.
source: Interestingly, we find that two critical regulators of necroptosis, CASP8 and ZBP1, are only found in tetrapods, suggestive of an additional innovation within the necroptosis pathway during the divergence of tetrapods.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenomic data in Figure 1C.

claim: The RHIM core tetrad was previously known to be conserved between humans and mice.
source: The RHIM core tetrad was previously known to be conserved between humans and mice (Riebeling et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Riebeling et al., 2022.

claim: RHIM-containing proteins have been identified in non-vertebrate animals and in fungi.
source: Additional RHIM-containing proteins have been identified in non-vertebrate animals and in fungi (Kajava et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kajava et al., 2014.

claim: RHIM proteins found in fruit fly and fungi are involved in antibacterial defense and cell death, respectively.
source: Interestingly, the RHIM proteins found in fruit fly and fungi are known to be involved in antibacterial defense and cell death, respectively, suggesting that RHIM-mediated interactions may be an ancient mechanism of innate immunity.
evidence: This is supported by knowledge from the literature and leads to an inference about ancient mechanisms.

claim: Vaccinia virus E3 prevents Z-DNA sensing by ZBP1.
source: For example, vaccinia virus E3 prevents Z-DNA sensing by ZBP1 (Koehler et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Koehler et al., 2021.

claim: Human cytomegalovirus UL36 promotes MLKL degradation.
source: human cytomegalovirus UL36 promotes MLKL degradation
evidence: This is supported by knowledge from the literature.

claim: Poxviruses encode an MLKL homolog to prevent RIPK3-mediated activation of host MLKL.
source: and poxviruses encode an MLKL homolog to prevent RIPK3-mediated activation of host MLKL (Petrie et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Petrie et al., 2019.

claim: Several viral mechanisms targeting RIPK3/RIPK1 are known to be species-specific and differ between humans and mice.
source: Intriguingly, several of these mechanisms are known to be species-specific and differ between humans and mice (Muscolino et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Muscolino et al., 2021 and Huang et al., 2015.

claim: RIPK1 function is central to determining cell fate downstream of TNF and TLR signaling.
source: The strong conservation of NF-κB activation by RIPK1 across species is consistent with the model in which RIPK1 function is central to determining cell fate downstream of TNF and TLR signaling (Clucas and Meier, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Clucas and Meier, 2023 and inference from the data.

claim: Some pathogens have evolved strategies to inhibit CASP8, leading to activation of RIPK3- and RIPK1-mediated necroptosis as a secondary cell death strategy.
source: Moreover, because some pathogens have evolved strategies to inhibit CASP8, RIPK3- and RIPK1-mediated necroptosis is activated as a secondary cell death strategy when CASP8 is inhibited (Remick et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Remick et al., 2023.
